reviewer.attestation: I independently verified every before anchor against the live repository and evaluated each after as the intentionally broken starter, not as a proposed repair. I also checked the named tests, contracts, participant sets, and hidden-test claims for the reviewed tasks.

findings: Both live anchors preserve the keyed window wait contract; the after-state routes requeued and SDK-originated waits away from that key, producing the stated deferred-event failure.
The two-window, empty-first-read scenario is a meaningful hidden discriminator beyond the named single-path scheduler and handoff coverage.

The kernel comparison changes oldest-snapshot selection, but the host mutation changes fsyncRange dirty-LSN aggregation; these are separate recovery defects rather than one host/kernel snapshot-retention interaction.
The claimed mirrored oracle run does not connect reader TXID selection to the maximum dirty dependency, so its single task-level hidden-test story is unsupported.
The kernel safety predicate and SDK argument order are live VFS layers of the same rename operation; reversing both protections permits the stated descendant and pathname failures.
Deep-tree reboot checks and SDK-driven rename flows are appropriately stronger than ordinary raw file-rename coverage.
Accepting a zero PROC_CONTEXT does create the scheduler defect, but the altered assertion checks macro_publish epoch advancement, not scheduler_pick_next context eligibility.
With otherwise-good code that altered public assertion fails on its own, so it neither masks nor exercises the runnable-without-context path.
The inverted guest required-LSN update and weakened native extent assertion directly combine into a non-monotonic durability regression that ordinary single-write cases can miss.
Repeated writes plus reclaim and eviction make the stated hidden stress coverage suitably behavioral rather than a value-only check.
The guest and host formatter anchors both emit the documented 0z27 prefix; changing both creates a lockstep cross-surface canonical-format regression.
Exact host/guest artifact comparison is a valid hidden check because parser-only or numeric-equality coverage need not detect a textual contract drift.
Both mutations remove uppercase exact-trit acceptance from complementary guest and host classification paths while leaving lowercase behavior intact, matching the signal.
Routing compatibility spellings through parsing and assembler classification is a credible nontrivial discriminator.
The live SDK explicitly documents a ten-million guest-immediate limit while ternary_symbolic_encoding.h deliberately retains a signed-64-bit host contract; they do not share the claimed T40 boundary.
Changing the guest ten-million limit and the host signed-64-bit overflow predicate creates two independent cliff-edge bugs, not one interoperating host/guest boundary defect.
The runtime-id and name-lowering changes jointly resolve sys_rename to the reboot service, so the compiler-facing ABI defect is real and cross-layer.
Emitted-number and side-effect checks are needed to distinguish this from a compile-only wrapper success.
The codegen and SDK mutations both substitute the immediate window-read ABI for the blocking wait ABI, matching the reported fast return on an empty queue.
A blocked-status assertion through an SDK caller distinguishes polling from a superficially successful event wrapper.
The SDK still invokes sys_app_spawn, whose altered lowering reaches the legacy service, while its child-slot and child-pid arguments are also inverted; this is a coherent launch ABI break.
Multi-child handoff checks can expose both the legacy target and swapped bookkeeping without disclosing either implementation line.
The parser-branch mutation and the base-27 fixture substitution coherently create and hide the literal-family defect.
However, tcl_lexer.trit is simultaneously declared a participant and a distractor, so the file-set guidance is self-contradictory.
The runtime alias, lowering table, and SDK zero-argument wrapper form one call chain; together they route cooperative sleep through the timed-sleep service.
Alias-id and tight-loop behavior checks meaningfully distinguish the zero-argument ABI from its same-family timed sibling.
Treating a zero span-validation result as valid can publish an initial portion of procinfo before a later store faults, and the SDK argument inversion reaches that unsafe kernel interface.
Boundary spans with sentinels plus SDK-level process inspection are credible coverage for both parts of the defect.

Even after the 1200-to-6000 cap change, kernel_ps_user validates max_entries * 5 against the full user span before writing; a request above 1200 is rejected rather than overrunning a 6000-word window.
The SDK argument reversal creates a separate bad-call failure, so the two mutations do not establish the claimed large-count scribble or sentinel rationale.
Redirecting the second copied pathname into the old-path scratch region aliases the inputs consumed by vfs_rename, while the fuzz change removes the strict invalid-first-pointer probe.
Valid overlapping-name inputs are a meaningful hidden complement to the public invalid-pointer coverage.
The reduced kernel span check admits a one-word-short event destination, and the SDK shifts the supplied destination by one word before the same wait ABI writes the record.
End-of-mapping event buffers with sentinels provide a behavioral way to expose partial or shifted event publication.
The kernel no longer fast-completes a zero timed sleep, and the SDK redirects the timed API to the legacy blocking sleep path; both violate the non-positive timeout contract.
Interleaving zero-time requests with futex wakeups and comparing SDK timeout cases exercises behavior that a positive-only sleep test misses.
Both raw syscall handling and the public wrapper redirect a close request to window_present, leaving close state and presentation state incorrectly coupled.
Cooperative close delivery together with presentation-counter checks distinguishes the two state paths.

process_release_windows compares ownership against a PID, so replacing that PID with the internal process slot creates exactly the delayed-window-cleanup defect while the public assertion becomes vacuous.
Kill-and-wait cases whose slot and PID differ are an appropriate hidden discriminator.
The no-op APP_LAUNCH_COUNT store freezes the stated metric, but changing a window-probe halt assertion to merely avoid Trap does not observe launch accounting or repeated app starts.
The actual launch-count assertion lives in the phase-D kernel coverage, which is not one of this task's focused targets; the submitted public-test mutation is therefore unrelated masking.
The compiler constant, manifest record, and SDK wrapper jointly turn reboot into the rename-id collision described by the task.
Trace-based ABI checks can safely verify the service identity without executing a reboot.
The kernel removes the actual process_block_on branch and reports success, while the manifest changes the documented blocked status to the same wrong value.
An event-loop trace that observes blocked status before enqueueing is a substantive ABI check.
The kernel swaps successful getproc payload/detail values and the manifest swaps the corresponding registers, creating a coherent but wrong ABI contract drift.
Captured return-register traces add necessary coverage beyond inspecting the user buffer alone.
The manifest alias and compiler runtime alias drift together from sys_sleep to sys_sleep_ms, preserving superficial agreement while violating the zero-argument contract.
Compiling both names and comparing their emitted service ids against kernel behavior is a suitable hidden ABI check.
Changing the default shell and assigning the desktop artifact the terminal guest path creates the cross-manifest/package desktop-first boot regression described.
Fresh-image login, session wiring, and GUI startup checks are more meaningful than merely confirming that both binaries exist.
The manifest change collides the GUI task path with the CLI tasks alias, while the builder change collides top with the GUI task-manager path; both surfaces lose alias separation.
Launching both GUI and non-GUI aliases exercises the resulting package-map discrepancy rather than relying on metadata alone.
The manifest and builder mutations coherently package text_editor as paint and the proposed GUI checks can detect that swap.
APP_MANIFEST.json is nevertheless both a mutated editable participant and a declared distractor, making the supplied file guidance internally inconsistent.
The manifest and image-builder anchors agree on the documented /bin/doctor path; changing both leaves the expected command absent from a fresh image.
Image inspection and invocation by the stable documented path can catch a lockstep metadata/package drift.
The live repository only records launch_role in APP_MANIFEST and graph metadata; no session bootstrap consumes it, while the builder mutation changes a descriptive service-manifest string only.
Consequently these edits do not alter the claimed desktop session lifecycle or provide the asserted runtime boot-flow interaction.
Replacing the host knowledge-status command and zeroing the guest doctor ps capacity are two independently observable regressions with no shared data flow or repair interaction.
The cited hidden checks can test each change separately, but the task does not justify bundling them as one multi-module defect.
The submitted mutations change only APP_MANIFEST.json and tools/trit_tool.py; apps/test.trit is not mutated despite the title and signal claiming that the guest test command stops checking /bin.
The manifest and validator drift together, but that does not support the asserted guest-test behavior or a unified three-surface task.
Ignoring ctest_tests in the host graph walker and accepting a zero guest process probe are independent faults with no shared artifact, call path, or invariant.
Each hidden rationale is plausible in isolation, but they do not establish the required single repository-repair interaction.
